title: Cloud configuration: which settings let attackers in, and would you notice if one changed?
short: Check Microsoft 365 and every cloud account against one free baseline this month, block public storage and long-lived keys at the top, and diff the results every week.
answer: This month, run CISA's ScubaGear against Microsoft 365 and a free posture check against each cloud, and fix public storage, long-lived access keys, open app consent and open external access first. Then lock those settings with organization-level guardrails and re-run the same checks every week, so a changed setting shows up as a diff rather than as an incident.
audience: IT, platform and security teams running Microsoft 365 with workloads in Azure, AWS or Google Cloud, in organizations of any size

blocks.title: If you only do five things

items.title: Measure against one published baseline this month.
items.text: Run CISA's free ScubaGear against Microsoft 365; it reads settings and changes nothing[^scubagear]. For clouds, Defender for Cloud's free Foundational CSPM checks Azure, AWS and Google Cloud against the Microsoft cloud security benchmark[^cspm].

items.title: Block public storage at the top.
items.text: Enforce S3 Block Public Access for the whole AWS organization[^s3org], set `AllowBlobPublicAccess` to false on every Azure storage account[^azanon] and enforce `storage.publicAccessPrevention` in Google Cloud[^gcpcons]. The DBIR counts data stores left online without access controls among the most common errors behind breaches[^dbir].

items.title: Replace long-lived keys with short-lived credentials.
items.text: AWS traces a large portion of security events to compromised long-term access keys[^awsssec]. In late 2025 attackers broke in with AWS keys suspected to have leaked in 2022[^th]. Move people to federated sign-in and workloads to roles or managed identities, then delete the keys.

items.title: Close app consent and external access in Microsoft 365.
items.text: Restrict user consent to verified publishers and low-risk permissions, with an admin consent workflow[^scuba]. Allow Teams external access only for named domains[^scubateams]: confirmed vishing over cross-tenant Teams calls rose 502% in a year[^mddr].

items.title: Turn the baseline into guardrails, then diff it weekly.
items.text: Enforce what must never change with AWS Organizations policies, Azure Policy and Google Cloud organization policies. Re-run the assessment every week and compare runs; ScubaGear's `Invoke-SCuBADiff` does this for Microsoft 365[^scubagear].

blocks.title: Adopt a baseline without breaking things

items.title: Pick one baseline per platform.
items.text: For Microsoft 365, SCuBA, or Baseline Security Mode, which every plan has in the admin center[^bsm]. For Azure, the Microsoft cloud security benchmark[^mcsb]; for AWS, Foundational Security Best Practices[^fsbp]; for Google Cloud, its security baseline constraints[^gcpbase].

items.title: Assess before you change anything.
items.text: Export every failing check. ScubaGear's first run also writes a template of your tenant's current settings[^scubagear].

items.title: Write down each exception.
items.text: Record why each failing setting stays, who owns it and when it ends. ScubaGear's YAML config holds these as exclusions, annotations or omissions[^scubagear].

items.title: Check the impact, then fix.
items.text: Start with the policies CISA marks as BOD 25-01 requirements[^bod]. Turn on each Baseline Security Mode setting whose impact report shows zero impact[^bsm], and start Azure Policy in audit mode.

items.title: Enforce, then re-run.
items.text: Switch audit to deny once the findings are fixed, test each guardrail on one account or OU first, and re-run the assessment to confirm.

blocks.title: Settings attackers go after
items: **Public storage.** Google's public access prevention revokes existing public access the moment you enforce it[^gcpcons]. Move public websites and downloads into a separate account or project before you enforce any of these settings.

**Access keys and shared keys.** Attackers reach Azure Blob Storage through exposed credentials, shared keys and SAS tokens[^mddr], and accounts accept their keys until `AllowSharedKeyAccess` is false[^azshared]. Google Cloud blocks service account keys in organizations created since May 2024[^gcpbase] and disables keys it finds exposed[^th]. Entra app secrets: see the privileged access sheet.

**Instance metadata.** IMDSv1 hands an instance's role credentials to any request that reaches it, including through SSRF flaws and open proxies[^imdsblog]. Require IMDSv2 by account default or declarative policy, find laggards with the `ImdsV1Enabled` metric, and add `ec2:RoleDelivery` to an SCP so IMDSv1 credentials stop working[^imds].

**Broad roles for workloads.** Generate policies from actual use with IAM Access Analyzer[^iambp] and remove wildcard actions, which Security Hub flags as IAM.1 and IAM.21[^fsbp]. For GitHub Actions deploying through OIDC, pin the role's `sub` condition to one repository and branch or environment[^ghoidc].

**Guests and external access.** Let only admins and Guest Inviters invite guests, limit guests' directory access, invite only from approved domains[^scuba] and block chats started by unmanaged Teams accounts[^scubateams]. In Google Cloud, `iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains` keeps IAM grants inside your organization[^gcpbase]. SharePoint links: see the DLP sheet.

**OAuth app consent.** Microsoft's managed default for new tenants still lets users consent to delegated permissions outside a list of mail, file, calendar and chat scopes[^consentpol]. Changing it keeps existing grants[^consent], so review those too. Stolen Salesloft Drift tokens opened Salesforce data at Google, Zscaler, Cisco and others in 2025[^dbir].

blocks.title: Guardrails and drift checks
items: **AWS.** SCPs cap what roles can do, RCPs what resources allow, and declarative policies set EC2 defaults such as IMDSv2 across accounts[^orgpol][^imds]. Test each on one OU before the whole organization.
**Azure.** Assign deny policies at a management group. Deny blocks new and updated resources but only marks existing ones non-compliant[^azdeny], so fix those separately.
**Google Cloud.** Organizations created before 3 May 2024 lack the security baseline constraints[^gcpbase]. Set them yourself, plus a policy that blocks 0.0.0.0/0 ingress, as Google advises[^th].

**Infrastructure as code.** Scan each Terraform or CloudFormation pull request with a policy checker such as Checkov[^checkov]. Run `terraform plan` on a schedule: a non-empty plan nobody started means a change outside the pipeline.
**The guardrails themselves.** Alert on changes to SCPs, policy assignments, organization policies, consent settings and Conditional Access. The logging sheet covers which logs to keep.

blocks.title: What changed in 2026
items: **Exploits overtook weak credentials in Google Cloud.** In late 2025, software flaws opened 44.5% of the Google Cloud intrusions in Google's data, weak or missing credentials 27.2% and misconfiguration 21%, down from 29.4%. Google thinks its secure defaults may explain part of the shift[^th]. Patch exposed workloads within the patching sheet's deadlines.

**ScubaGear 2.0 is out.** CISA's October 2026 release adds a Security Suite baseline for Defender, Purview, Exchange Online and Teams and scores risky apps[^scubanews]. The Entra baseline now requires blocking risky AI agents[^scuba]. Re-run it and update your config file.

**Microsoft 365 moved toward secure defaults.** Baseline Security Mode, in the admin center since November 2025, covers phishing-resistant MFA for admins, legacy authentication and app consent, with impact reports[^bsm]. Tenant Configuration Management, generally available since April 2026, monitors over 200 settings across six workloads[^tcmga].

**S3 tightened two defaults.** Since November 2025 one AWS Organizations policy can enforce Block Public Access for every account[^s3org]. Since April 2026 new buckets reject SSE-C[^ssec], which attackers with stolen keys had used to re-encrypt victims' objects[^awsssec].

blocks.title: What you can skip
items: **A paid CSPM before the free checks.** ScubaGear is public domain[^scubagear], and Defender for Cloud's Foundational CSPM is free for Azure, AWS and Google Cloud[^cspm]. Buy attack path analysis after the basics are closed.
**Perfecting 90-day key rotation.** Security Hub checks for it[^fsbp], but AWS advises not creating long-term keys at all[^awsssec]. Remove them instead.

**Mapping to every framework first.** Microsoft notes that its benchmark's mappings to CIS, NIST or PCI DSS don't by themselves mean compliance[^mcsb]. Fix against one baseline, then map for the auditor.

blocks.title: Mistakes that cost the most
items: **Trusting a new default to fix old resources.** An IMDSv2 account default leaves existing instances alone[^imds], and consent changes keep existing grants[^consent].
**Running workloads in the AWS management account.** SCPs and RCPs don't restrict it[^orgpol].
**Giving the deploy pipeline admin rights.** UNC6426 turned a stolen GitHub token into AWS administrator access in under 72 hours, because the pipeline's CloudFormation role could create roles[^th].
**Exposing a test resource "just for a day."** Microsoft measured a median of 5.3 hours from an exposed container's start to the first exploit attempt[^mddr].

blocks.title: What this looks like at your size

columns.title: Small team, no security staff
items: Turn on each Baseline Security Mode setting with zero impact[^bsm].
Ask your IT provider for a monthly ScubaGear report and the list of consented apps and guests.
Keep all cloud accounts under one organization or management group, with public storage blocked at the top.

columns.title: Growing, with IT or security staff
items: Run ScubaGear weekly from a scheduled job and post the diff to the team channel.
Connect every cloud account to one posture tool and give each finding an owner and a due date.
Make infrastructure as code the only write path, and keep console write access for emergency roles.

columns.title: Enterprise or regulated
items: US federal civilian agencies must meet BOD 25-01's mandatory SCuBA policies and report results to CISA[^bod].
Feed tenant drift and posture findings into the SIEM, with a fix time per severity.
Review changes to SCPs, Azure Policy and organization policies like Tier 0 code, with two people.
